response.text:
Assume \(m_1\) is the displayed full model

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{1i}+\beta_2X_{2i}+\varepsilon_i,
\]

where \(Y=\) kid’s IQ, \(X_1=\) mom’s IQ, and \(X_2=\) mom’s age.

---

### (1) Sample size

Residual df \(=431\). The full model has 3 parameters: intercept, \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\). Thus

\[
n-3=431 \implies n=434.
\]

\[
\boxed{n=434}
\]

---

### (2) Fitted model \(m_1\)

\[
\boxed{\widehat{\text{Kid IQ}}
=17.596+0.604(\text{Mom IQ})+0.388(\text{Mom age})}
\]

---

### (3) LS estimate of \(\beta_1\) and interpretation

\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=0.604}
\]

Interpretation: Holding mom’s age fixed, a 1-point increase in mom’s IQ is associated with an estimated \(0.604\)-point increase in the child’s IQ.

---

### (4) Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) at 5%

Test statistic:

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_1}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=\frac{0.604}{0.0587}
\approx 10.29.
\]

Degrees of freedom: \(431\).

Since

\[
|t|=10.29 \gg t_{0.975,431}\approx 1.97,
\]

we reject \(H_0\). The p-value is extremely small, essentially \(<2\times 10^{-16}\).

\[
\boxed{\text{Mom's IQ is a statistically significant predictor of kid's IQ at }5\%.}
\]

---

### (5) Overall \(F\)-statistic for \(m_1\)

The overall null is

\[
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\text{at least one of }\beta_1,\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Using

\[
F=\frac{R^2/k}{(1-R^2)/(n-k-1)},
\]

with \(R^2=0.2036\), \(k=2\), and \(n-k-1=431\),

\[
F=\frac{0.2036/2}{0.7964/431}
\approx 55.09.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{F\approx 55.1 \text{ on }(2,431)\text{ df}}
\]

with p-value \(<2.2\times 10^{-16}\).

---

### (6) \(t\)-statistic for testing \(\beta_2=0\)

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_2}{SE(\hat\beta_2)}
=\frac{0.388}{0.326}
\approx 1.19.
\]

\[
\boxed{t\approx 1.19}
\]

This is not significant at the 5% level; the two-sided p-value is about \(0.235\).

---

### (7) Hypotheses for the nested `anova(m2, m1)` test

Assuming \(m_2\) is the reduced model with mom’s IQ only,

\[
m_2: Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\varepsilon,
\]

and \(m_1\) is the full model with mom’s IQ and mom’s age,

\[
m_1: Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+\varepsilon,
\]

then the nested ANOVA tests whether mom’s age adds explanatory power after controlling for mom’s IQ.

Thus

\[
H_0:\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

---

### (8) Blanked nested ANOVA quantities and conclusion

Using the residual standard error,

\[
\text{MSE}=18.26^2\approx 333.43.
\]

For the full model,

\[
RSS_{\text{full}}=431(18.26)^2
\approx 143707.3.
\]

Since the comparison adds one variable, the partial \(F\)-statistic equals the square of the corresponding \(t\)-statistic:

\[
F=t^2\approx (1.19)^2\approx 1.42.
\]

The numerator df is \(1\), and the denominator df is \(431\). Thus the nested ANOVA table is approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{Model} & \text{Res.Df} & RSS & Df & \text{Sum Sq} & F & p\\
\hline
m_2: X_1 \text{ only} & 432 & 144180 & & & & \\
m_1: X_1+X_2 & 431 & 143707 & 1 & 472 & 1.42 & 0.235
\end{array}
\]

So the key blanks are approximately

\[
\boxed{Df=1,\qquad F\approx 1.42,\qquad p\approx 0.235.}
\]

Conclusion: Since \(p\approx 0.235>0.05\), we fail to reject \(H_0\). There is not sufficient evidence that mom’s age improves the model after accounting for mom’s IQ.
